   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?

   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?

   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?

   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?

   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?

   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: Arm fits most Rule Breaker traits: it is the top dog in CPU architecture for an emerging AI-everywhere market, has a sustainable advantage in its software ecosystem, strong 52-week price momentum (+38%), and is widely called overvalued. Weaker points are low name recognition among consumers and control by SoftBank rather than a founder-led team.
summaries.buffett: Arm has a durable moat, 97.5% gross margins and no borrowings, but it has been public only since 2023, its earnings have been uneven, and it trades at about 240 times trailing GAAP earnings. Buffett would likely admire the toll-booth royalty model but find no margin of safety at the price.
summaries.munger: The royalty-on-every-chip model and the ecosystem lock-in are the kind of great business Munger liked, but inverting reveals real failure paths: RISC-V, conflict with licensees after launching its own chips, China exposure and Qualcomm litigation. The valuation of roughly 100 times forward earnings leaves little room for error.
summaries.lynch: Arm is a clear fast grower (revenue +22.8% in FY2026) with a simple story: more chips, higher royalties per chip and now its own data center chips. But the P/E is several times the growth rate, insiders sell and the share count rises, and Wall Street follows it closely, so it fails most Lynch value tests.
summaries.fisher: Arm scores well on Fisher's growth points: a long runway, heavy and productive R&D ($2.8bn in FY2026, delivering Armv9, CSS and the AGI CPU), and management willing to sacrifice near-term margin for long-term position. Concerns are its strained relations with some licensees and limited minority-shareholder influence under SoftBank.
summaries.graham: Arm fails nearly every Graham defensive-investor test: no dividend, a short public history, a P/E above 200 on trailing earnings and a price-to-book near 29. Its only Graham-friendly traits are its size and strong balance sheet.
summaries.thiel: Arm is close to a Thiel-style monopoly: it started with a big share of a small market (low-power mobile chips in the 1990s) and expanded to own nearly all smartphones, with network effects and a cornered architecture. The open-source RISC-V alternative and its new competition with its own customers are the main questions about durability.
summaries.gerstner: Arm is a direct beneficiary of the AI compute platform shift, with data center royalties more than doubling year on year and over $2bn of AGI CPU commitments. Gerstner's discipline on valuation and cost would flag the 49 times sales multiple, 34% R&D growth and stock-based pay.
summaries.druckenmiller: The liquidity backdrop is unhelpful (US CPI 3.7% and talk of Fed hikes) and the stock fell about 30% in a month into mid-October 2026 despite record results and a guidance beat. Upcoming catalysts such as the AGI CPU ramp and the Qualcomm verdict could move it, but conviction for a concentrated position is hard to justify at this valuation.
summaries.smith: Arm is a good company by Fundsmith's tests on gross margin, low capital needs and no debt, but its GAAP returns on capital (about 14%) and free-cash-flow conversion are only moderate, and at a 0.6% FCF yield it is clearly 'overpaying'.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula Arm ranks poorly: its earnings yield (EBIT/EV) is about 0.4%, and GAAP return on capital is only moderate despite the asset-light model.
summaries.akre: Arm has the first leg of Akre's stool (an extraordinary business with a toll-like royalty model) and a long reinvestment runway, but management's capital allocation is unproven (a costly push into silicon, talk of buying Eliyan) and the price is far from reasonable.
summaries.pabrai: Arm is not a Dhandho bet: there is no temporary distress, the odds are not 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much', and the price assumes years of rapid growth. Its moat would appeal, but the downside is large if growth disappoints.
summaries.wood: Arm fits ARK's disruptive-innovation themes as an AI infrastructure layer spanning data centers, edge devices, autonomous cars and robotics, with costs per unit of compute falling. It is less of a pure play on a new technology platform than ARK's typical holdings because its base business is mature smartphone royalties.
summaries.ackman: Arm is simple and predictable at its core with a dominant market position and no debt, matching several Pershing Square criteria. But SoftBank's roughly 90% control rules out activist influence, and free cash flow is small compared with the $250bn value, so it fails the reasonable-price test.
summaries.sleep: Nomad's 'scale economics shared' does not quite fit: Arm captures more value per chip through higher royalty rates rather than passing savings back to customers. Its long-term destination looks strong, but the pricing approach invites customer pushback and RISC-V adoption.
summaries.valentine: Arm addresses a huge market with a product that solves a painful problem (computing within tight power budgets), which is what Valentine looked for. Its market is enormous and growing with AI, though as a 35-year-old company it is far from Sequoia's early-stage territory.
summaries.nash: Arm passes Nash's trend, story and balance-sheet steps: it sells into AI infrastructure, has net cash, grows over 20% a year and scores 85 on the 13-category scorecard. It fails the instant-kill rule on a trailing GAAP operating margin of about 17%, expenses grew faster than revenue in FY2026, it faces Qualcomm litigation, and the price is far above a 12% DCF with a PEG above 3.

momentum.evidence: Arm shares rose 38.43% in the 52 weeks to Oct 14, 2026 (close $238.01), versus about a 20% one-year total return for the SPY S&P 500 ETF, though they fell from $307.49 on Oct 2.

g4.evidence: SoftBank owns roughly 90%, Apple, NVIDIA, Google, Samsung and Intel were anchor investors in the 2023 IPO, and CEO Rene Haas is a respected chip industry veteran.

g6.evidence: Commentators routinely call Arm overvalued at about 49 times sales and around 100 times forward earnings.

simple.evidence: The licence-plus-royalty model is easy to grasp, but judging royalty rates, CSS adoption, the AGI CPU and RISC-V competition takes specialist chip knowledge.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose from $2,027m (FY2021) to $4,920m (FY2026) but dipped in FY2023, and operating income swung from $671m (FY2023) to $111m (FY2024) to $900m (FY2026).

integrity.evidence: Shareholder letters are detailed and guidance is generally met, but SoftBank's control limits minority influence, and heavy stock-based pay (GAAP vs non-GAAP R&D gap of $865m in FY2026) dilutes owners.

b6.evidence: Moving into its own AGI CPU is a strategic bet rather than copying peers, but reported talks to buy networking startup Eliyan at a steep valuation in October 2026 raised empire-building concerns.

roic.evidence: Arm uses no debt and has an asset-light model, but trailing GAAP ROIC is about 14% and ROE about 13% (StockAnalysis), held down by stock-based pay and a large equity base.

fcf.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow was $979m ($1,524m operating cash flow less $545m capex) against $904m net income, but FY2025 FCF was only $178m on $792m net income.

b10.evidence: Arm pays no dividend and its market value has grown from about $54bn at the September 2023 IPO to about $254bn, far more than the earnings it retained.

safety.evidence: At $238 the stock trades at about 240 times trailing GAAP earnings and 29 times book value, well above any conservative intrinsic value estimate.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E near 100 and a PEG of about 3.3 (StockAnalysis) is high even for 20%+ revenue growth and a strong moat.

mu5.evidence: The ecosystem makes sudden failure unlikely, but RISC-V, customers designing their own cores, China exposure (18% of FY2026 revenue) and conflict over its own silicon are real ways to erode it.

reinvest.evidence: Arm can reinvest in new architectures, CSS and data center silicon, where it has over $2bn of AGI CPU commitments, with a long runway in AI computing.

ly2.evidence: Arm is a fast grower: revenue rose 22.8% in FY2026 and 22% in Q1 FY2027, with a simple story of higher royalties per chip plus data center expansion.

ly3.evidence: The forward P/E of about 100 is roughly four times the ~26% expected EPS growth for FY2027.

runway.evidence: Data center royalties more than doubled year on year in Q1 FY2027, and Arm is expanding into PCs, cars and its own chips.

ly7.evidence: Executives including CFO Jason Child have sold under 10b5-1 plans, and diluted shares rose from 1,025m (FY2022) to 1,078m (June 2026 quarter).

ly8.evidence: Arm is one of the most-followed AI stocks, with about 43 analysts covering it.

fi2.evidence: Arm moved from Armv8 to Armv9, then to Compute Subsystems and in 2026 to its first in-house AGI CPU.

fi3.evidence: R&D produced Armv9 and CSS, which lifted royalty revenue 20.5% to $2,613m in FY2026, and the AGI CPU, which has won Meta, OpenAI and Cloudflare as customers.

fi4.evidence: Arm signs nearly every major chip company, but its sales approach has led to disputes, notably the Qualcomm litigation since 2022.

longterm.evidence: Management raised GAAP R&D 34% to $2,776m in FY2026 and is building its own silicon, accepting lower near-term margins for a bigger long-term position.

gr1.evidence: Arm had $4,920m of FY2026 revenue and a market value of about $254bn.

ni10.evidence: Arm reported profits for FY2021-FY2026 (net income $388m to $904m), but audited results for earlier years under SoftBank's private ownership are not in its SEC filings.

gr4.evidence: Arm has paid no dividend since its 2023 IPO.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $0.38 (FY2021) to $0.85 (FY2026), but no ten-year per-share record exists because Arm relisted only in 2023.

gr6.evidence: The share price is about 240 times trailing GAAP earnings, far above 15 times.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 243 times P/B of about 29 is around 7,000, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Arm's power efficiency and ecosystem are far ahead in mobile, but compared with x86 in servers or RISC-V in embedded it is better, not ten times better.

timing.evidence: AI data centers are limited by power, which favours Arm's efficient CPUs; Arm-based servers reached an estimated 21% of 2025 shipments (IDC).

th3.evidence: Arm started in low-power chips for devices like the Apple Newton and Nokia phones, won nearly all of mobile, and is now expanding into PCs, cars and data centers.

team.evidence: CEO Rene Haas is a capable chip veteran who has executed well since 2022, but Arm is not founder-led and SoftBank's Masayoshi Son holds control.

th5.evidence: Arm has direct licensing relationships with essentially every chip designer and hyperscaler, plus a royalty system tied to every shipped chip.

durable.evidence: The Arm software ecosystem should hold in phones for decades, but RISC-V and customers designing their own cores could erode it over 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: Arm saw early that power efficiency would rule data centers, but rivals such as RISC-V vendors and NVIDIA see the same opportunity.

trend.evidence: Arm is a leading beneficiary of AI: its Neoverse cores power AWS Graviton, Google Axion, Microsoft Cobalt and NVIDIA Grace, and data center royalties more than doubled in Q1 FY2027.

dr1.evidence: Q1 FY2027 non-GAAP EPS rose 28% to $0.45 and Q2 guidance beat consensus, but some brokers cut price targets (one from $475 to $340).

dr2.evidence: AGI CPU commitments above $2bn and doubling data center royalties should show in results within 18-24 months beyond current expectations.

dr4.evidence: September 2026 US CPI of 3.7% raised talk of Fed hikes, and with a 5-year beta of about 3.8 Arm is very sensitive to tighter money.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include the AGI CPU production ramp, the Qualcomm jury verdict in October 2026 and Q2 FY2027 results guided to $1.38bn of revenue.

dr7.evidence: The moat supports conviction, but a 30% drop in a month, litigation and a P/E near 100 make a large concentrated position risky.

gm.evidence: FY2026 GAAP gross margin was 97.5% ($4,799m gross profit on $4,920m revenue).

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow of about $1.51bn on a market value of about $254bn is roughly a 0.6% FCF yield.

gb2.evidence: Trailing operating income is under 0.4% of the roughly $251bn enterprise value (EV/EBIT about 281).

pa2.evidence: The recent 30% share-price fall reflects valuation, rates and litigation worries, not a setback in the business, which reported record revenue.

pa4.evidence: The business is very unlikely to fail and has net cash, but at about 49 times sales the shares could fall a long way if growth slows.

wo1.evidence: Arm is a core AI infrastructure supplier, with its CPU designs and AGI CPU used alongside AI accelerators in data centers and for AI on phones.

wo2.evidence: Arm-based chips lower compute cost per watt as volumes grow, but Arm itself is raising royalty rates rather than cutting prices.

wo3.evidence: Arm spans AI, autonomous vehicles and robotics through its automotive and edge AI designs, though AI computing is the main engine.

wo4.evidence: Moving from IP royalties to selling whole chips multiplies Arm's revenue per data center socket, but a market many times larger in five years is unproven.

ac3.evidence: Arm has no commodity inputs and no debt, but smartphone volumes (43% of FY2026 royalties came from mobile) are hurt by memory prices and consumer demand.

ns1.evidence: Arm is increasing royalty rates per chip with Armv9 and CSS rather than sharing scale savings with customers.

ns4.evidence: Arm should be bigger in data centers in 10-20 years, but RISC-V and conflict with licensees make a clearly stronger position uncertain.

va2.evidence: Arm solves the painful problem of getting high performance within tight power budgets, which decides phone battery life and data center power costs.

tn1.evidence: Arm sells the CPU infrastructure layer for AI computing, built from the start for power-efficient computing rather than retrofitted.

tn2.evidence: The market still sees Arm as a smartphone IP licensor, while it is becoming a data center silicon supplier with over $2bn of AGI CPU commitments.

tn3.evidence: Arm is a $250bn UK/US-listed company founded in 1990, not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn4.evidence: Revenue grew in each of the last three years to $4,920m, FY2026 net income was $904m, and it has $3,888m of cash and short-term investments and no borrowings.

tn5.evidence: Cash has exceeded debt every quarter and recent quarters were FCF-positive (Q4 FY2026 $186m, Q1 FY2027 about $665m), but quarterly FCF has been lumpy and I could not check every quarter.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 22.8% in FY2026 and 22% in Q1 FY2027.

tn7.evidence: FY2026 revenue growth of 22.8% plus an FCF margin of 19.9% ($979m / $4,920m) gives about 43.

tn8.evidence: In FY2026 revenue grew 22.8%, but operating expenses (gross profit minus operating income) grew 27.6%, from $3,055m to $3,899m.

tn9.evidence: It fails the instant kill of an operating margin below 20% (18.3% in FY2026, about 17% trailing), and short interest of 16.2m shares is about 15% of the roughly 10% free float not held by SoftBank.

tn10.evidence: Arm faces Qualcomm litigation (an appeal of its Nuvia loss and a breach trial that went to a jury in October 2026) plus US-China export-control risk around Arm China.

tn11.evidence: Arm provides CPU designs that help chip makers build power-efficient processors, charging upfront licence fees plus a royalty on every chip shipped; customers choose it for its software ecosystem.

tn13.evidence: Total 85: cash vs debt 10, revenue growth 10, operating margin 5 (17.3%), short interest 5 (1.5% of shares but higher of free float), institutional ownership 0 (9.3%, SoftBank owns ~90%), revenue faster than expenses 0, return vs S&P 10 (from $51 IPO price in 2023 to $238), moat 10, CEO 5, pricing power 10, secular trend 10, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue fell slightly in FY2023 ($2,679m vs $2,703m), operating margin did not expand steadily (25% FY2023, 3.4% FY2024, 18.3% FY2026), and FCF fell to $178m in FY2025.

tn15.evidence: Arm has no borrowings and so no interest burden, a current ratio of about 5.3 and equity of $8,286m far exceeding liabilities.

tn18.evidence: Rene Haas has executed well since 2022, but he has about four years as CEO, is not a founder and has not made notable open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: Arm has usually beaten its revenue guidance, including Q1 FY2027 ($1.29bn vs $1.27bn expected, non-GAAP EPS $0.45 vs $0.40), but some reports framed that quarter as an earnings miss on a GAAP basis.

tn21.evidence: Operating margin fell from 20.7% (FY2025) to 18.3% (FY2026), and executives sold shares under 10b5-1 plans while the stock ran up.

tn22.evidence: Arm has $4.9bn of revenue, is profitable and has not raised equity since its IPO.

tn24.evidence: At about 49 times sales and 168 times free cash flow, the price implies sustained growth well above the 22-23% Arm currently delivers.

tn25.evidence: Using ~22.5% growth and an ~18% average FCF margin for five years, a 12% discount rate and 4% terminal growth gives about $27 per share, far below $238.

tn26.evidence: The forward P/E of about 100 is far above chip peers, and the PEG is about 3.3 (StockAnalysis), well above 1.
